# Databases {#sec-databases}

::: {.callout-note title="From the exam description"}
Knowledge of bioinformatics' most important databases and understanding
their hierarchy and relationships.
:::

## Introduction

Bioinformatics depends on public databases, and knowing what each one
contains, where its data come from and how much to trust it is a core
skill. A useful distinction is between **primary (archival)** databases,
which store data as submitted by the experimentalists, and **secondary
(derived or curated)** databases, which add analysis, classification or
expert annotation on top of the primary data.

Nucleotide sequences are archived by the International Nucleotide Sequence
Database Collaboration (INSDC). It has three partners, GenBank (NCBI), ENA
(EMBL-EBI) and DDBJ, which exchange data daily. Raw sequencing reads are
stored in the SRA/ENA. Genome resources such as Ensembl, the UCSC Genome
Browser and NCBI RefSeq build curated, non-redundant gene models and
annotations on top of these archives [@cunningham2022]. Most protein
sequences are never determined directly: they are translated from
predicted genes. UniProt [@uniprot2023] collects them into UniProtKB. That
database has two parts: Swiss-Prot, which is manually reviewed and
annotated, and TrEMBL, which is annotated automatically. UniProt also
provides clustered sets (UniRef) and an archive of all sequences
(UniParc).

On top of the sequences sit databases that group proteins into families
and domains. Pfam builds profile HMMs from curated seed alignments
[@sonnhammer1997; @mistry2021]. InterPro integrates Pfam and a dozen other
family and site databases into a single resource [@paysanlafosse2023].
Experimentally determined structures are archived in the PDB
[@berman2000]. Structures are classified hierarchically into domains,
folds and superfamilies by SCOP, CATH and ECOD
[@murzin1995; @sillitoe2021; @cheng2014]. Since 2021 the AlphaFold
Database has provided predicted structures for almost every protein in
UniProt [@varadi2022]. Function is described with controlled vocabularies,
above all the Gene Ontology [@ashburner2000; @go2023]. Pathways are
described in KEGG and Reactome, and interactions in resources such as
STRING, IntAct and BioGRID [@szklarczyk2023].

These resources are tightly connected through cross-references, so a gene
in Ensembl links to its protein in UniProt, the domains in InterPro, the
structures in the PDB and the GO terms describing its function. Each step
away from the primary data adds value but also adds possible errors. A
classic problem is that automatically transferred annotations can
propagate one wrong assignment to thousands of entries. Good practice is
to know which evidence a particular annotation is based on. Every January,
*Nucleic Acids Research* publishes a database issue with updated
descriptions of most of these resources.

## Key concepts

- Primary nucleotide archives: INSDC (GenBank, ENA, DDBJ), SRA/ENA reads
- Genome databases and browsers: Ensembl, UCSC, NCBI RefSeq
- Protein sequence databases: UniProtKB (Swiss-Prot vs. TrEMBL), UniRef, UniParc, metagenomic sequence sets
- Protein families and domains: Pfam, InterPro (member databases), CDD
- Structure: PDB/wwPDB, EMDB; structure classifications SCOP, CATH, ECOD; predicted structures (AlphaFold DB)
- Function and pathways: Gene Ontology, KEGG, Reactome
- Interactions: STRING, IntAct, BioGRID
- Expression and proteomics repositories: GEO, ArrayExpress, PRIDE
- Curation vs. automatic annotation; error propagation; redundancy
- Retrieval systems: Entrez, EBI Search, programmatic access (APIs)
